title: Cambodia's energy, remittance, and credit shock tests whether returning workers can become a demographic dividend before the care and human-capital window closes
source_unit: World Bank, Cambodia Economic Update June 2026: Forever Young? Cambodia's Demographic Transition and the Road to Vision 2050
geography: Cambodia; national macroeconomy, households, returning migrant workers, labor market, demographic transition, human capital, care economy, and trade system

observations.period: 2025–2026; energy, remittance, credit, and household-consumption shock

denominator.unit: Cambodian economy and household-consumption simulation frame

growth_projection.unit: percent projected real GDP growth in 2026

remittance_share.unit: percent of GDP in remittances in 2025, down from a 6% average in 2019–2024

consumption_effect.unit: percent average reduction in household consumption under the fuel-price scenario

poverty_effect.unit: percentage-point increase in the modeled poverty rate under the fuel-price scenario; about 1.1 million people could be pushed into poverty

transmission.value: About 80% of modeled welfare losses are transmitted indirectly through higher prices of goods and services

observations.method: World Bank economic update combining macroeconomic indicators, household-consumption simulations, remittance and credit data, and policy analysis; the fuel-price result is a conditional scenario rather than an observed treatment effect.
observations.uncertainty: The projected growth rate and fuel scenario depend on conflict duration, prices, exchange rates, income distribution, substitution, and policy response; average consumption effects do not identify which households reduce food, mobility, health, or cultural spending.
observations.subgroup: Remittance-receiving households, fuel- and transport-intensive households, poor and near-poor families, domestic firms, and workers returning from Thailand are likely to face different exposure and buffers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Foreign direct investment, international reserves, transfers, substitution, and targeted support may cushion the shock; a modeled average is not a realized poverty trajectory.

observations.period: 2025–2026; returning migrant workers and labor-market reintegration

denominator.unit: Cambodian migrant returnees and labor-market reintegration program context; no single respondent denominator is reported

returnees.value: Nearly one million migrant workers returned, following a sharp fall in remittance income

jobs_added.unit: jobs added in 2025, including about 401,000 in the formal sector

placements.unit: returnees reportedly placed in employment through competency assessments and direct factory referrals

mismatch.value: Returnees were typically older, male, and rural, while labor demand was concentrated in younger, female-intensive manufacturing near Phnom Penh

observations.method: World Bank labor-market and reintegration assessment using reported employment, placement, demographic, sector, and location patterns.
observations.uncertainty: Placement counts do not establish job quality, wages, retention, safety, commuting, household income replacement, or whether returnees chose or could sustain the reported jobs; the source does not follow the same worker over time.
observations.subgroup: Returning migrants, older male and rural workers, younger female-intensive manufacturing workers, employers near Phnom Penh, and households previously dependent on remittances.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid placement can preserve household income and create a bridge to formal employment even if initial jobs are imperfect; informal work or migration may remain rational where local alternatives are weak.

working_age_peak.unit: projected year when Cambodia's working-age population share peaks

workers_added.unit: million additional workers in the labor force by 2050 relative to 2024, under the report's projection

support_ratio.unit: workers aged 15–64 per person aged 65+ projected from 2024 to 2050

human_capital_return.unit: percent estimated increase in future earnings potential from closing the human-capital gap

policy_window.value: Barely about 17 years remain to convert the demographic dividend into higher productivity and better jobs

observations.method: World Bank demographic projections, human-capital comparison, and growth decomposition; projections are conditional on fertility, mortality, migration, participation, productivity, and policy assumptions.
observations.uncertainty: A demographic window does not automatically produce growth: job creation, education, health, care, migration, productivity, and fiscal capacity determine whether the projected labor supply becomes a dividend or a burden.
observations.subgroup: Young workers, future older people, rural and urban populations, women, migrants, employers, caregivers, and public systems that must support a lower old-age support ratio.
observations.counterinterpretation: A larger working-age population can support growth even with partial human-capital gaps, and automation, migration, or longer working lives can alter the projected support ratio; the report's urgency is not a guaranteed outcome.

observations.period: 2026–2050; care, human capital, and structured mobility as growth infrastructure

denominator.unit: Cambodian human-capital, care, labor-mobility, and trade-policy system

care_route.value: Formal childcare and eldercare can create decent jobs, unlock female labor productivity, and build the next generation's human capital

mobility_route.value: Structured, higher-return migration pathways and trade diversification are presented as complements to domestic human-capital investment

human_capital_gap.value: Cambodia's HCI+ health, education, and employment components remain below structural, upper-middle-income, and high-income peer benchmarks

capacity_control.value: Education quality, TVET, health, care-economy formalization, labor-market institutions, and fiscal buffers are treated as productivity investments rather than only social spending

observations.method: World Bank special-focus synthesis linking demographic projections, human-capital indicators, labor-market institutions, care-economy recommendations, structured migration, and trade diversification.
observations.uncertainty: Policy recommendations and peer comparisons do not establish implementation, service affordability, care quality, worker bargaining power, gender equality, or durable household outcomes; the estimated earnings return is model-dependent.
observations.subgroup: Women and caregivers, children, older people, TVET students, returning migrants, employers, rural provinces, and households relying on formal or informal care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formalizing care may improve quality and employment but can also raise prices or displace trusted informal arrangements; structured migration can expand opportunity while creating origin-community loss or dependence.

related_sources.claim: World Bank Cambodia country platform provides the country-program and economic context for the update.
World Development Indicators provide complementary demographic, labor, and macroeconomic data used in World Bank analysis.

boundary: This comparative record adds a shock-to-demography-to-capacity route: energy and remittance disruption, household purchasing power, returning-worker reintegration, demographic timing, human capital, care infrastructure, structured migration, and fiscal or labor-market institutions. It does not infer individual worker trajectories, job quality, benefit receipt, care outcomes, causal effects of a reform, or durable household recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank Cambodia Economic Update PDF reviewed for the 2026 growth projection, remittance and fuel-price shock, household-consumption simulation, returning-worker placement, demographic projections, human-capital gap, care-economy route, and structured-migration recommendations.
